sheet.line: Rockefeller Gratin: Oysters, Bacon, Creamed Spinach, Breadcrumbs

classic.text: Oysters Rockefeller was created at Antoine's in the French Quarter of New Orleans and is credited to Jules Alciatore, son of the founder Antoine Alciatore. Most accounts date it to 1899 (a few say 1889; the earliest firm record cited is a 1909 newspaper advertisement), and the usual story is that he used local oysters when imported snails were hard to get. It was named for John D. Rockefeller, the richest American of the day, for the richness of the sauce; the green is also tied to the colour of money. The classic is oysters on the half shell under a rich green sauce with breadcrumbs, baked or broiled. Antoine's keeps its recipe secret and its cooks have long denied that it holds spinach; most later versions use spinach.

facts.text: Gratin comes from the French verb gratter, to scrape: the word first meant the crust scraped from the cooking pot, and now names a dish baked or broiled until a browned crust forms on top, often of breadcrumbs or cheese. Au gratin does not mean with cheese.
